\section{Monte Carlo Design and Results}\label{app:mc}
\setlength{\emergencystretch}{2em}% allow looser lines in the online appendix

This appendix documents the two Monte Carlo designs behind Section~\ref{sec:ident} and Online
Appendix~\ref{app:obs}. Design~A asks what alternative experimental designs identify when they use the same total
compute. Design~B simulates an industry of labs that choose compute and allocations, and asks which
production-function estimators recover the technology from the models they release. Everything is simulated. The
truth is the technology of \citet{besiroglu2024chinchilla}: $E=1.8172$, $A=482.01$, $B=2085.43$, $\alpha=0.3478$ and
$\beta=0.3658$, so that $a=0.513$, $\gamma=0.178$, $\sigma^*=0.737$, and the compute-optimal ratio at $10^{24}$ FLOP
is $M^*=18.1$ tokens per parameter ($\ln M^*=2.898$). ``Bias'' is the Monte Carlo mean error and ``RMSE'' the
root-mean-squared error around the truth. No estimator is started at the true parameters. The first version of
this paper included the truth among the nine starting values of the Chinchilla-form fit, and its industry
estimators started at the truth; Table~\ref{tab:app-mc-starts} and the Design~B discussion report what removing
those starts changes.

\subsection{Design A: What Alternative Designs Identify}\label{app:mc-designA}

\emph{Setup.}---Every design has 90 runs, ten on each of nine compute budgets that match Chinchilla's nominal
IsoFLOP budgets ($6\times10^{18}$ to $3\times10^{21}$ FLOP), and hence the same total training compute,
$5.1\times10^{22}$ FLOP. The designs differ only in where the runs sit on their isocost lines
(Table~\ref{tab:app-mc-designs}): near the expansion path, as in a compute-optimal ladder; spread by IsoFLOP
profiles or a factorial grid, as in a designed experiment; spread by allocation errors with standard deviation $v$
in $\ln(D/N)$ at given compute, as by optimizing labs that err; or tilted systematically by labs that follow
Kaplan's allocation rule. Log loss carries normal noise with standard deviation 0.0075, the residual standard
deviation of the Besiroglu fit on the 240-run Chinchilla extraction. The residuals are heavy-tailed (their
MAD-based standard deviation is 0.0049) and bundle seed noise, digitization error and misspecification, so 0.0075
is an upper value for pure seed noise. Noise is realized after inputs are chosen, the case of
\citet{zellner1966specification}.

We compare three estimators. The primal estimator is the Huber ($\delta=10^{-3}$) fit of $\ln L$ used by
\citet{hoffmann2022training} and \citet{besiroglu2024chinchilla}, with $\kappa=1$, minimized inside a parameter box
from nine starting values drawn at random over the region of Hoffmann et al.'s initialization grid. The dual
estimator reads the path slope $a$ from the optima (or the IsoFLOP minima) and $\gamma$ from the frontier $L^*(C)$,
and recovers $\alpha=\gamma/a$ and $\beta=\gamma/(1-a)$; it identifies the exponents only through optimality and
$\kappa=1$. The third is a profile likelihood for $\sigma^*$ in the generalized family
$L=E+(AN^{-a_1}+BD^{-b_1})^{\kappa}$ with $\kappa$ free, on a 29-point grid over $[0.05,0.99]$, with the likelihood
ratio measured against the unrestricted optimum. At each grid point the optimizer starts from the members of the
observationally equivalent family of Proposition~\ref{prop:fd} that reproduce the on-path fits of the primal and
dual estimators; without these starts it produced spurious rejections at the edges of the grid.

\emph{On-path data do not identify the technology through the primal estimator.}---When every run is exactly
compute-optimal ($v=0$), 87 percent of fits end on a corner, with one power-law term switched off, and the RMSE of
$\hat\sigma^*$ is 0.27, against 0.004 for an IsoFLOP design spanning $\pm16\times$ the optimal size and 0.005 for the
factorial grid at the same compute (Table~\ref{tab:app-mc-designs}, Panel~A). The corners are not optimization
failures: no fit at $v=0$ has a higher Huber objective than the true parameters, so the data are fitted as well by a
technology with one input switched off as by the truth, the non-identification of
Proposition~\ref{prop:ident}(i)--(ii). Near the path the failure is a ridge: at $v=0.02$ the median error of
$\hat\sigma^*$ is $-0.12$, and its 5--95 percent range is $[0.34,0.75]$. The normalized condition number of the
information matrix at the truth rises from $1.4\times10^{3}$ in the designed experiments to $1.5\times10^{7}$ at
$v=0.02$ and is infinite at $v=0$. As $v$ rises to 0.05, 0.1 and 0.2, the RMSE of $\hat\sigma^*$ falls to 0.089,
0.025 and 0.015 (Figure~\ref{fig:designs}, panel~A). The compute-optimal ratio is the more demanding object once
optimality is not imposed: the RMSE of $\ln\hat M^*(10^{24})$ is 28 at $v=0$, 4.6 at $v=0.1$, 2.0 at $v=0.3$ and
0.59 at $v=1$, against 0.16 under the IsoFLOP design. At $v=0.3$ the 5--95 percent range of $\ln\hat M^*$ is
$[-0.40,6.34]$, a factor of about 850 in $M^*$. These are the finite-sample counterparts of the information rates
in Proposition~\ref{prop:ident}(iii).

\emph{Starting values matter only near the path.}---With the truth among the starts, as in the first version, 26
percent of on-path fits and 51 percent at $v=0$ ended on a corner; with nine random starts, 72 and 87 percent do
(Table~\ref{tab:app-mc-starts}). With 64 random starts the corner shares fall to 18 and 56 percent, and the RMSEs of
$\hat\sigma^*$ on the path, at $v=0$ and at $v=0.05$ (0.19, 0.30 and 0.071) are within 10 percent of the first
version's. For $v\ge0.1$ and for the designed experiments the start set makes no difference. The truth therefore
did not flatter the near-path designs much; what it hid is that on a ridge the estimate depends on where the
optimizer starts. With nine starts, 7 percent of fits at $v=0.05$ stop at a higher objective than that of the
truth, and 64 starts remove these failures. We keep nine starts, the number used in the first version, as the
baseline.

\emph{With $\kappa=1$ imposed, apparent precision at intermediate $v$ is functional form.}---For $0.1\le v\le0.3$ the
primal RMSE of $\hat\sigma^*$ (0.013 to 0.025) is no better than that of the dual estimator (0.012), which uses
only the path. The reason is analytic: with $\kappa=1$, $\alpha+\beta=\gamma/[a(1-a)]$, and $a(1-a)$ is flat near
$a=1/2$ (0.2498 at the truth), so $\sigma^*=2/(2+\gamma/[a(1-a)])\approx2/(2+4\gamma)$ is pinned down by the
on-path frontier elasticity. Freeing $\kappa$ removes that information (Table~\ref{tab:app-mc-designs}, Panel~B;
Figure~\ref{fig:app-mc-profile}). The 95 percent profile set for $\sigma^*$ is the whole grid in 91 percent of
on-path replications, 95 percent at $v=0$ and 79 percent at $v=0.05$. Larger allocation errors first rule out poor
substitutes. At $v=0.1$ the set still contains all of $[0.50,0.95]$ in 93 percent of replications but excludes
some value at or below 0.5 in 72 percent; at $v=0.3$ its median bounds are $[0.42,0.99]$. The upper end goes last: the set
contains every $\sigma^*\ge0.9$ in 76 percent of replications at $v=0.3$ and 45 percent at $v=0.5$. The asymmetry
follows from the Harberger-triangle approximation of Section~\ref{sec:ident-onpath}: an error $\delta$ in $\ln M$
costs a Farrell loss of about $(1-\sigma^*)\delta^2/(4\sigma^*)$, which is large when inputs are poor substitutes
and vanishes as $\sigma^*\to1$, so small losses are consistent with any elasticity near one. The set becomes
informative at $v=1$ (median bounds $[0.69,0.79]$) and in the designed experiments ($[0.729,0.745]$ for IsoFLOP
$\pm16\times$ and $[0.727,0.746]$ for the factorial grid), and it covers the truth in 93 to 100 percent of
replications in every design. Under Kaplan beliefs the set is the whole grid in 21 percent of replications. On the
range searched in the first version, $[0.50,0.95]$, the flat shares match the first version except on the path (94
against 88 percent) and under Kaplan beliefs (84 against 77 percent), where the additional starting value from the
dual fit removes optimizer failures at the edges of that range.

\emph{The dual estimator is precise on the path but inherits any systematic allocation error.}---On the path its
RMSEs are 0.0005 for $a$, 0.011 for $\sigma^*$ and 0.009 for $\ln M^*$. When labs optimize against Kaplan's beliefs
($N\propto C^{0.73}$), the same estimator is biased by $+0.217$ in $a$, $-0.088$ in $\sigma^*$ and $-3.92$ in $\ln
M^*$, understating $M^*$ about 50-fold. The primal estimator on the same data is roughly unbiased but weakly
identified (RMSE of $\hat\sigma^*$ 0.10; the Wald covariance is computable in 77 percent of replications).

\emph{On the path, standard inference is either wrong or uninformative.}---The Wald covariance is numerically
singular, or the fit is at a corner, in 79 percent of on-path replications. The pairs bootstrap as usually
implemented, with every draw warm-started at the full-sample estimate, covers $\sigma^*$ in 44 percent of 150
replications (Monte Carlo standard error 4 percentage points). In a separate check with 60 replications and 49
draws, restarting every draw also from the nine random starting values raises coverage from 33 to 78 percent,
still short of nominal, and yields a median interval width of 0.43, against 0.016 under the IsoFLOP design. With
designed variation all methods agree: Wald and bootstrap coverage is 95 to 97 percent for the IsoFLOP $\pm16\times$
and factorial designs and at $v=1$.

\emph{Noise.}---What counts as near-optimal depends on $v$ relative to the noise and on the number of runs
(Table~\ref{tab:app-mc-noise}). The RMSE of $\hat\sigma^*$ under the IsoFLOP design is 0.0024, 0.0036 and 0.0078
at noise standard deviations of 0.005, 0.0075 and 0.015; at $v=0.3$ the profile set contains all of $[0.50,0.95]$
in 38, 65 and 90 percent of replications. The seed noise we measure in our own experiment
(\textcolor{red}{[TBD-m9: seed standard deviation of $\ln L$]}) places it within this range. Digitizing the losses
as in the Epoch extraction barely matters for an IsoFLOP design (RMSE 0.0041 against 0.0036).

Heteroskedastic and clustered noise leaves the ranking of designs intact but breaks inference that assumes
independent errors. In this variant the noise standard deviation is proportional to $(ND)^{-1/4}$, larger for small
models and short runs, and half of each run's variance is shared within its compute budget (shared data order) or,
in the factorial grid, within its model size (one training trunk). The RMSE of $\hat\sigma^*$ is 0.0042 under the
IsoFLOP design, 0.0052 under the factorial grid, 0.022 at $v=0.3$ and 0.25 on the path, and the profile set is still
the whole grid in 61 percent of on-path replications. But Wald intervals that assume independence cover $\sigma^*$
in only 82, 74 and 61 percent of replications under the IsoFLOP, factorial and $v=0.3$ designs, and profile sets
calibrated by $\chi^2_1$ in 71, 82 and 91 percent. Inference must allow for dependence within budgets or training
trunks, as the preregistered analysis of our experiment does with a wild cluster bootstrap over trunks
(Section~\ref{sec:tech:experiment}).

\subsection{Design B: A Simulated AI Industry}\label{app:mc-designB}

\emph{Setup.}---Forty labs each produce six generations of models. In each generation a lab releases one to four
models whose compute budgets are roughly $8\times$ apart. Productivity is Hicks-neutral and equals
$\omega_{ft}=0.15(t-1)+x_{ft}$, where the lab component follows $x_{ft}=0.8\,x_{f,t-1}+\xi_{ft}$ with stationary
standard deviation 0.25; seed noise has standard deviation 0.05 in $y=-\ln(L-E)$. The dispersion of $\omega$ is
assumed, chosen to match the 41-fold within-developer 90--10 ratio in effective compute of
\citet{mertens2026secret}; TFP growth of 0.15 per generation is also assumed. A lab-generation's log budget is
$c_{ft}=\bar c_t+h_f-p_{ft}+\nu_{ft}$, where $\bar c_t$ grows by $\ln3$ per generation from $10^{21}$ FLOP, $h_f$ is
lab size (standard deviation 0.7), $p_{ft}$ is an observed compute-price shifter (0.4), and $\nu_{ft}$ is noise
(0.4). Four compute rules map productivity into budgets: (a) exogenous budgets; (b) funding that responds to
current productivity ($+2x_{ft}$); (c) a loss target that the lab reaches by buying compute; and (d) compute
provisioned one generation ahead ($+2x_{f,t-1}$), the timing assumption of \citet{ackerberg2015identification}. Labs
minimize lifetime compute given inference demand $T=3D^*(c)\theta$ with $\ln\theta\sim N(0,0.8^2)$, so that the mean
log wedge is 0.46, and make allocation errors with standard deviation 0.2 in $\ln(D/N)$. Variants add release
selection (about 18 percent of trained models unreleased), classical measurement error in $\ln D$ (standard
deviation 0.15), data-augmenting lab heterogeneity, and a flagship-only sample. The estimators, applied to released
models, are listed in Table~\ref{tab:app-mc-industry}. $E$ is known to all of them except the pooled Huber fit that
mimics current practice in machine learning. Every estimator starts from data-based values; relative to the first
version, whose least-squares estimators started at the truth, the biases of $\hat\gamma$ and of TFP growth change by
at most 0.003. Under the loss-target rule the pooled criterion has several local optima, and the bias of the
pooled estimate of $a$ moves from $-0.03$ to $-0.06$.

\emph{Transmission bias is diluted but not removed by common fixes.}---Pooled nonlinear least squares with generation
effects overstates $\gamma$ by 0.023 (13 percent) under funding and 0.018 under predetermined budgets, and understates
it by 0.053 (30 percent) under a loss target (Table~\ref{tab:app-mc-industry}, Panel~A). With one model per
lab-generation under funding the bias is $+0.118$, matching the closed form of Proposition~\ref{prop:A-transmission}
applied to this design (0.118). Lab fixed effects remove about two-thirds of the bias under funding and four-fifths
under predetermined budgets, but not under the target rule ($-0.022$), and almost none of it with flagships only
($+0.113$), because $\omega$ is persistent rather than fixed. The bias loads on the frontier elasticity, not on the
allocation: the regression of $\ln N$ on $\ln C$ recovers $a$ with $\lvert\text{bias}\rvert\le0.003$ in every scenario
(Panel~B, IV row).

\emph{Within-family variation is the observational analog of an IsoFLOP experiment.}---Lab $\times$ generation
fixed effects, which use only the size menu within a lab-generation, are unbiased for $\gamma$, $a$ and TFP growth
under every compute rule ($\lvert\text{bias}\rvert\le0.002$), because siblings share $\omega$ and their tier and
inference-demand differences are exogenous. The estimator needs at least two released siblings, is unavailable with
flagships only, and is hurt by measurement error in $D$ (bias in $\ln M^*$ of $-0.33$ at an error standard deviation
of 0.15, similar to lab fixed effects, $-0.28$). Estimators in the spirit of \citet{ackerberg2015identification}
remove the transmission bias when the timing assumption is right ($\lvert\text{bias}\rvert\le0.002$ for $\gamma$
with lagged instruments only) and fail when it is wrong ($-0.027$ under the target rule if current compute is
treated as predetermined). Both variants, however, use the current within-family deviations of inputs as
instruments, without which the lagged moment set is under-identified, so they borrow the same within-family
variation; the lagged-instrument version is also about five times less precise for $a$ (RMSE 0.12 to 0.13 against
0.025 to 0.028). The simulation therefore does not show that proxy or timing estimators work on flagship-only panels.

\emph{First-order-condition estimators mistake inference demand for technology.}---Stacking the within-family loss
equation with the training-only first-order condition ($w=1$) leaves the exponents essentially unbiased but biases
$\ln M^*$ by $+1.25$ to $+1.28$ under every compute rule (Panel~D), overstating $M^*$ about 3.5-fold. This is close to the
closed form $2\,\mathbb{E}[\ln w]/(\alpha+\beta)=2\times0.457/0.714=1.28$: the first-order-condition residual is the
wedge of Proposition~\ref{prop:A-wedge}, and ignoring it makes over-trained models look like evidence that data are
cheap. A noisy usage proxy for $T$ (log noise 0.3) removes the bias ($-0.02$ to $-0.03$, RMSE at most 0.05). The
instrumental-variable estimator that reads $M^*$ off the observed path inherits the same contamination (median bias $+1.27$ to
$+1.32$), although its median bias for $\gamma$ is small ($-0.002$ to $+0.005$; median absolute error 0.027 to
0.031) when releases are not selected.

\emph{Current practice absorbs more than half of algorithmic progress into the scaling law.}---The pooled Huber fit
with $E$ free and no time effects, the specification common in the machine-learning literature, understates TFP
growth by 0.081 to 0.090 of a true 0.150 per generation under rules (a), (b) and (d) (Panel~C), and overstates $\ln
M^*$ by 0.53 to 0.64. Holding $E$ at the truth isolates the scale-attribution channel of
\citet{nagy2013statistical}: the same pooled regression still misses 36 to 43 percent of TFP growth and steepens the
frontier by 0.050 to 0.059. Roughly two-thirds of the absorbed progress is attributed to scale and one-third to a
downward-biased asymptote $\hat E$.

\emph{Selection and its correction interact with transmission.}---With exogenous budgets and a notability threshold
for release, pooled estimates understate $\gamma$ by 0.008 and overstate TFP growth by 0.011; a
\citet{heckman1979sample} correction, which assumes that the inputs of unreleased models are observed and that a
release-policy shifter is excluded, roughly halves both. Under predetermined budgets, selection ($-$) and
transmission ($+$) offset (net $+0.01$), and the correction raises the bias to $+0.018$ by removing only the
selection part. Selection also invalidates the compute-price instrument (median bias $-0.022$ and $-0.033$). The
industry calibration is illustrative, not estimated; only signs and rankings should be read from Design~B, and the
magnitudes scale with the assumed ratio of productivity-driven to total variance in compute.

\subsection{Verification of the Transmission and Selection Formulas}\label{app:mc-formulas}

Table~\ref{tab:app-mc-transmission} checks the transmission-bias formula of Proposition~\ref{prop:A-transmission}
against simulations with $10^6$ draws per case. The simulated slopes match the closed form to within $10^{-3}$ in
all twelve cases, on the expansion path and with lifetime-optimal allocations. The sign of the bias follows the
compute rule: exogenous budgets give $\gamma$, funding and predetermined budgets overstate it, and a common loss
target drives the slope to zero. The forward and reverse regressions bracket $\gamma$ under exogenous budgets and
dispersed targets, but under funding and predetermined budgets both exceed it. In samples of 240 lab-generations the
nominal 95 percent OLS interval covers $\gamma$ in 95 percent of samples under exogenous budgets, but in 53 percent
under mild funding, at most 4 percent under stronger funding, and 16 percent under predetermined budgets with
$\lambda=1$; these coverage rates depend on the assumed exogenous dispersion of compute. The residual dispersion
also behaves as predicted: under funding with $\lambda=2$ the standard deviation of the OLS residual is 0.229,
against 0.255 for productivity plus noise, so cross-lab regressions understate TFP dispersion.

Outcome-based release biases the compute slope toward zero (Proposition~\ref{prop:selection}). With exogenous
budgets and an absolute release threshold, the slope falls from 0.178 to 0.112, 0.082 and 0.057 as 25, 50 and 75
percent of runs are dropped. Combined with a funding rule ($\lambda=2$), the net bias moves from $+0.100$ without
selection to $-0.006$ and $-0.046$ with 50 and 75 percent dropped, so its sign is ambiguous, as the theory implies.
The allocation identities with factor-augmenting productivity and the wedge identity of
Proposition~\ref{prop:A-wedge} hold in the simulation to within $10^{-14}$.

\emph{Reproducibility.}---The code is in \texttt{code/analysis/m6\_montecarlo} (entry point \texttt{run\_v2.py}; the
start-value checks are \texttt{designA\_startcheck.py} and \texttt{designB\_startcheck2.py}). Every design cell
seeds its own random-number generator, so results do not depend on the number of processes, and the simulated data
are identical to those of the first version. On four CPU processes Design~A takes 18 minutes, the bootstrap check 3
minutes, Design~B 6 minutes and the 64-start check 15 minutes.
